L500: ### 4.2 Order-preserving functions with a fixed point
L501: 
L502: Let $\T_{n}$ be the monoid of all functions $f:[n]\to[n]$ (where $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$). A function is called order-preserving if $i_{1}\leq i_{2}$ implies $f(i_{1})\leq f(i_{2})$. Denote by $\Op_{n}$ the monoid of all order-preserving functions $f:[n]\to[n]$. We denote by $\OF_{n}$ the monoid of all order-preserving functions $f:[n]\to[n]$ with the fixed point $f(n)=n$.
L503: ###### Example 4.3.
L504: 
L505: The monoid $\OF_{3}$ consists of the following $6$ elements:
L506: 
L507:  | $$\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&2&3\\
L508: 1&2&3\end{array}\right),\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&2&3\\
L509: 1&3&3\end{array}\right),\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&2&3\\
L510: 2&3&3\end{array}\right)$$  |
L511:  | $$\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&2&3\\
L512: 1&1&3\end{array}\right),\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&2&3\\
L513: 2&2&3\end{array}\right),\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&2&3\\
L514: 3&3&3\end{array}\right)$$  |
L515: Clearly, $\OF_{n}$ is a submonoid of $\Op_{n}$. Note the analogy with the definition of the monoid $\PT_{n}$ of all partial functions on an $n$-element set. The monoid $\PT_{n}$ can be identified with the submonoid of $\T_{n+1}$ which consists of all functions $f:[n+1]\to[n+1]$ such that $f(n+1)=n+1$.
L516: To the author’s knowledge, the monoid $\OF_{n}$ has not been studied before. In this section we will discuss some properties of this monoid with emphasis on its structure as a reduced $E$-Fountain semigroup.
L517: Let $f\in\OF_{n}$. Recall that the kernel of $f$ - $\ker(f)$ - is the equivalence relation on its domain defined by $(i_{1},i_{2})\in\ker(f)$ if and only if $f(i_{1})=f(i_{2})$. Since $f$ is order-preserving, the kernel classes of $f$ are intervals - if $i_{1}\leq i_{2}\leq i_{3}$ and $(i_{1},i_{3})\in\ker(f)$ then $(i_{1},i_{2})\in\ker f$ also.

Choose $x_{i}$ to be the maximal element of $K_{i}$. Since $f(n)=n$ it must be the case that $y_{l+1}=n$ and $x_{l+1}=n$. Now, set

L530: The number of elements of $\OF_{n}$ is ${\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{k}^{2}={2n-2\choose n-1}}.$
L531: ###### Proof.

L533: We sum over all pairs $X,Y\subseteq[n-1]$ with the same size. The final equality follows from [cite63†22 , Example 1.1.17]. ∎
L534: Another observation will be useful. A function $f:[n]\to[n]$ is called order-increasing if $i\leq f(i)$ for every $i\in[n]$. In particular, if $f$ is order-increasing then $f(n)=n$. Let $\C_{n}$ be the submonoid of $\OF_{n}$ which consists of all order-preserving and order-increasing functions $f:[n]\to[n]$. This monoid is called the Catalan monoid because the size of $\C_{n}$ is the $n$-th Catalan number [cite64†8 , Theorem 14.2.8].
L535: It is well-known that $\C_{n}$ is a $\Jc$-trivial monoid [cite34†31 , Proposition 17.17]. Given $X=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{l}\}$ and $Y=\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{l}\}$ we say that $X\leq Y$ if $x_{i}\leq y_{i}$ for $1\leq i\leq l$. It is easy to see that $f_{X,Y}\in\OF_{n}$ is order-increasing if and only if $X\leq Y$ (see also [cite28†19 ]). Therefore,
L536:  | $$\C_{n}=\{f_{X,Y}\in\OF_{n}\mid X\leq Y\}.$$  |

L538: In the rest of this section we consider several properties of the monoid $\OF_{n}$ and its algebra.
L539: #### Idempotents
L540: 
L541: Let $X=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{l}\}$ and $Y=\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{l}\}$ be two subsets of $[n-1]$. It is well-known (see [cite64†8 , Theorem 2.7.2]) that a function $f$ is an idempotent if $f(i)=i$ for every $i\in\im(f)$. In view of (cite65†2 ) and the fact that $\im(f_{X,Y})=Y\cup\{n\}$ it follows that $f_{X,Y}$ is an idempotent if and only if $y_{1}\leq x_{1}$ and $x_{i-1}<y_{i}\leq x_{i}$ for $2\leq i\leq l$.

L553: Next, we turn to describe the $\Jc$-classes. Recall that the rank of a function $f$ is the size of its image. For $f_{X,Y}\in\OF_{n}$ we have $\rank(f_{X,Y})=|X|+1=|Y|+1$.
L554: ###### Lemma 4.6.
L555: 
L556: Let $f_{X,Y},f_{Z,W}\in\OF_{n}$ then $f_{X,Y}\,\Jc\,f_{Z,W}\iff\rank(f_{X,Y})=\rank(f_{Z,W})$.
L557: ###### Proof.

L564: In conclusion, we obtain a neat description for the “eggbox” diagrams of $\OF_{n}$ (see [cite43†12 , Section 2.2] for the meaning of an “eggbox” diagram). Both the $\Rc$-classes and the $\Lc$-classes in $J_{k}$ are indexed by subsets $Z\subseteq[n-1]$ with $|Z|=k$. For every $Z\subseteq[n-1]$ with $|Z|=k$ we have an $\Rc$-class

L572: #### Reduced $E$-Fountain structure
L573: 
L574: Set $E=\{f_{X,X}\mid X\subseteq[n-1]\}\subseteq E(\OF_{n})$. Note that $E$ does not contain all the idempotents of $\OF_{n}$, but it is precisely the set of idempotents of $\C_{n}$. According to cite66†4.5 , we know that

L577: for every $X,Y\subseteq[n-1]$ with $|X|=|Y|$. Therefore, every $\Lc$-class and every $\Rc$-class contains an element of $E$. Since $\Lc\subseteq\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{E}$ and $\Rc\subseteq\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{E}$, we deduce that every $\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{E}$-class and every $\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{E}$-class contains an element of $E$ so $\OF_{n}$ is an $E$-Fountain semigroup.

L516: According to Theorem cite70†5.2 , Proposition cite71†5.4 and Lemma cite72†5.6 we obtain:
L517: ### Theorem 5.7
L518: 
L519: The graph \(\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\) with composition as defined in Definition cite56†3.7 is a category (with zero morphisms) and for every commutative unital ring \(\Bbbk \) there is an isomorphism of algebras \(\Bbbk {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\simeq \Bbbk _{0}\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\).
L520: ### Remark 5.8
L521: The fact that \(\Bbbk {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) and \(\Bbbk _{0}\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\) are Morita equivalent (i.e., their module categories are equivalent) follows from the well-known Dold–Kan correspondence [cite73†3 , cite74†13 ].
L522: It is possible to show that \(\Bbbk {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) is Morita equivalent to the algebra of the category of sets \(\{1,\ldots ,k\}\) for \(1\le k\le n\) and all the order-preserving functions between them — this is the simplex category [cite75†17 , Section VII 5] truncated at n.
L523: According to the Dold–Kan theorem, this algebra is Morita equivalent to the contracted algebra of the skeleton of \(\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\) which is Morita equivalent to \(\Bbbk _{0}\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\) itself (see [cite76†36 , Proposition 2.2]). The contracted algebra of the skeleton is the algebra of a straight line quiver with n vertices and the relations are that each composition of successive arrows equals 0.
L524: See also the Lack–Street equivalence [cite77†15 ] and [cite78†34 , Example 4.9].

L554: The graph \(\mathcal {C}({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n})\) associated with \({{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) can be described as follows. The objects are in one-to-one correspondence with the set of idempotents \(E=\{e_{X}\}\) (where \(X\subseteq [n]\) such that \(n\in X\)). For every \(f_{Y,X}\in {{\,\mathrm{\mathcal {O}}\,}}_{n}\) we associate a non-zero morphism \(C(f_{Y,X})\) from \(e_{X}\) to \(e_{\widetilde{Y}}\).
